leads.title: Small daily habit changes could add years to your life, study finds
leads.summary: A University of Sydney study published in eClinicalMedicine on January 13, 2026 followed more than 59,000 older adults in the UK Biobank for just over eight years. People with the poorest habits who made three small changes together - about 5 more minutes of sleep a night, about 2 more minutes of exercise a day and a small diet improvement - gained about one year of life. Bigger but still modest changes (24 more minutes of sleep, under 4 more minutes of exercise, better diet) were linked to up to four more years free of serious disease such as heart disease, cancer, dementia or type 2 diabetes. Researchers say to start with small, realistic steps.
leads.source: Powers Health / University of Sydney study

leads.title: A Kargil teacher turns old war bunkers into classrooms where children can live history
leads.summary: Mohd Mustafa Kamal, a 41-year-old teacher from Wakha village near Kargil in Ladakh, converted a derelict military bunker at his school into a history lab called the Cave Classroom, so students can feel history instead of only reading it. He also made a Museum Classroom with local artefacts and a parliament-style seating plan for civics. He received the National Teachers Award 2026 from President Droupadi Murmu on September 5, 2026, among 48 teachers honoured. Innovator Sonam Wangchuk praised his bottom-up approach.

leads.title: Berlin mapped 900,000 street trees. Now 12,000 people water them.
leads.summary: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Amanda Gläser-Bligh named her street tree Linda. Linda is a linden, eight years old, growing outside Gläser-Bligh’s apartment building in Charlottenburg, and once a week during Berlin’s hot months, Gläser-Bligh makes a couple of trips up and down the stairs with a watering can until she has carried 20 liters (about five gallons) of water to Linda’s roots. Passersby sometimes stop and stare. They usually end up asking what she’s doing, and most of them, once they find out, look up at the tree a little differently. Berlin has nearly a million street trees, and like cities across Europe, it’s watching them struggle through increasingly hot summers. A project called Gieß den Kiez , which translates to “water your neighborhood” in German, is trying to close the gap between what the city’s maintenance crews can do and what the trees need, by giving ordinary people a map, a reason, and a social framework for showing up with a watering can. Twelve thousand people have signed up. 900,000 trees color-coded by thirst and updated in real time Developed by CityLAB Berlin , the Gieß den Kiez app tracks more than 900,000 trees across the city and calculates each tree’s water needs based on its age, species, and local rainfall. Color-coding shows which trees are in critical condition. Saplings, which lack the deep root networks of mature trees, need more frequent watering to survive and are flagged accordingly. Volunteers can log a watering, see when a tree was last watered by someone else, and find the locations of Berlin’s public water pumps.
